title: Remember Lot’s Wife
paragraphs:
Remember Lot’s Wife
The Lesson That Haunted Me Long After I Closed My Bible
There are some verses in Scripture that comfort you.
Some inspire you.
Some strengthen you.
And then there are the verses that stop you in your tracks and refuse to let you go.
For me, one of those verses is only three words long.
Three words.
No explanation.
No sermon.
No commentary.
Just three words spoken directly by Jesus Christ Himself:
“Remember Lot’s wife.” (Luke 17:32)
That is all He said.
Yet those three words carry the weight of eternity.
Because Jesus was not simply asking us to remember a woman.
He was warning us not to become her.
The first time I truly wrestled with those words, I realized something uncomfortable.
I had always assumed Lot’s wife was judged because she looked back.
But the longer I studied Scripture, the more I understood that the problem was never merely where her eyes turned.
The problem was where her heart remained.
The account begins in Genesis 19 as God prepares to judge Sodom and Gomorrah because of their wickedness.
The Hebrew text repeatedly emphasizes the severity of their corruption. The city had become a picture of rebellion against God.
Yet even in judgment, God displayed mercy.
Angels were sent to rescue Lot and his family.
Genesis 19:17 records the command:
“Escape for your life. Do not look back and do not stop anywhere in the valley.”
The Hebrew phrase for “do not look back” is אַל־תַּבִּיט אַחֲרֶיךָ (al-tabbit achareikha).
It means far more than a casual glance.
The verb carries the idea of gazing with regard, consideration, attachment, longing, or focused attention.
This was not simply a warning against turning one's head.
It was a warning against turning one's heart.
God was leading them out.
But part of her was still inside the city.
And that is where this story stops being about Lot’s wife and starts being about us.
Because how many of us have physically left certain sins while emotionally remaining attached to them?
How many of us have walked away from toxic relationships but secretly wished we could return?
How many of us have prayed for freedom while quietly mourning the chains God was breaking?
How many of us have asked Jesus to transform our lives while still romanticizing the life He rescued us from?
The tragedy of Lot’s wife is not that she wanted to see Sodom one last time.
The tragedy is that Sodom was still living inside her.
Genesis 19:26 says:
“But Lot’s wife, behind him, looked back, and she became a pillar of salt.”
The Hebrew text uses the phrase וַתַּבֵּט מֵאַחֲרָיו (vattabet me'acharav).
Again, this is not describing a fleeting glance.
It implies deliberate regard.
A lingering look.
A heart unable to let go.
A soul divided between salvation and destruction.
She was being rescued by grace.
Yet she was grieving what grace was taking away.
That reality hit me harder than I expected.
Because I realized how often I have wanted God to save me while allowing me to keep the very things destroying me.
I wanted the peace of Christ without surrender.
The blessings of God without obedience.
Freedom without separation from the things enslaving me.
But Jesus never calls people to partial surrender.
He calls them to Himself.
When Jesus referenced Lot’s wife in Luke 17, He was teaching about His return.
The Greek text simply says:
Μνημονεύετε τῆς γυναικὸς Λώτ
(Mnēmoneuete tēs gynaikos Lōt)
“Remember Lot’s wife.”
The word μνημονεύετε (mnēmoneuete) is an active command.
It means continually remember.
Keep remembering.
Never forget.
Jesus intentionally reached back into Genesis because He knew future generations would struggle with the same temptation.
The temptation to follow Him while still looking back.
The temptation to move toward Heaven while remaining emotionally attached to the world.
The temptation to trust Christ for salvation while refusing full surrender.
Immediately after this warning, Jesus says:
“Whoever seeks to preserve his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life will keep it.” (Luke 17:33)
The connection is unmistakable.
Lot’s wife wanted both.
She wanted rescue and remembrance.
Deliverance and attachment.
Freedom and nostalgia.
But eventually every disciple faces the same choice.
Will we follow Jesus forward?
Or will we keep looking backward?
One of the most dangerous spiritual conditions is not open rebellion.
It is divided affection.
A heart that wants Christ but also wants Egypt.
A heart that wants Heaven but misses Sodom.
A heart that wants grace while secretly longing for the old life.
That is why Jesus later declared:
“No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.” (Luke 9:62)
He was not describing perfection.
He was describing direction.
A true disciple may stumble.
A true disciple may struggle.
A true disciple may fall.
But a true disciple keeps moving toward Christ.
The older I get, the more I understand that following Jesus often means grieving things that once defined you.
Not because they were good.
But because they were familiar.
Sin can become familiar.
Brokenness can become familiar.
Bitterness can become familiar.
Shame can become familiar.
Even pain can become familiar.
And sometimes God must call us away from what is familiar so He can lead us into what is holy.
That journey is not always easy.
But it is always worth it.
Because the Gospel is not merely about escaping judgment.
The Gospel is about becoming new.
The Apostle Paul wrote:
“Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation.”
The Greek phrase is:
καινὴ κτίσις (kainē ktisis)
A new creation.
Not repaired.
Not renovated.
Not slightly improved.
New.
Entirely new.
This is the beauty of the Gospel.
Jesus never asks us to save ourselves.
He saves us.
He rescues us.
He transforms us.
He rewrites us.
The same God who called Abraham.
The same God who rescued Lot.
The same God who raised Christ from the dead.
Still changes lives today.
Maybe that is why the story of Lot’s wife lingers in my heart.
Because it forces me to ask difficult questions.
What am I still looking back at?
What am I still mourning that God has called me to leave behind?
What has Jesus already delivered me from that I secretly wish I could revisit?
Be honest.
This question reaches deeper than most of us want to admit.
And perhaps that is exactly why Jesus said, “Remember Lot’s wife.”
Because every generation needs the reminder.
The danger was never behind her.
The danger was inside her.
And the same warning still echoes through every human heart today.
Your testimony may encourage someone who feels alone in their battle today.
If we truly desire to glorify God, we should joyfully support the work that spreads His truth, equips believers, reaches the lost, and advances the Gospel to more people every day.
Because one day you will realize something Lot’s wife never did.
The future God has prepared for you is infinitely greater than anything He asked you to leave behind.
And sometimes the holiest thing you can do is refuse to look back.
